name: Wendy Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the supermarket in our market town, the only big one for fifteen miles, so everybody comes through my till sooner or later. I do four days a week, mostly tills, and I train the new starters on the checkouts because I'm patient and I don't panic when the scanner dies. On Saturdays I run my own cake stall at the farmers' market in the square.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the stall more than the till, if I'm honest, because it's mine. I use AI every day for it, it writes my labels with the allergens, works out my prices when butter goes up, and answers the order messages when I'm on shift. What wears me out at the supermarket is the clock, everything is timed, even toilet breaks. My husband Ken works on a dairy farm outside town, so we're both up before five most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a lot of people were frightened for nothing. At church I'd say hard work still counts, which I believe. At the till I'd probably joke that the robot never came for my job after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. The AI I use already saves me about five hours a week on the stall, and that keeps working in this picture. My job at the supermarket is steady, we've got about four months saved, and Ken's farm job isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my four days at the supermarket because it pays the bills and the training role gives me a bit extra. I'd grow the stall slowly, maybe add a second market in the next town on Sundays, and use the AI to manage the orders. I'd put the stall money into a separate account for a proper bakery one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, really. Busy, but happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the stall bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred clear in a good month, more in December with the Christmas cakes. Last year I did forty Christmas cakes and the AI kept track of who'd paid and who wanted marzipan. Ken says I should charge more, and he's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The price of butter, honestly. It went up a third in two years and I can't put my prices up as fast. But that's business, you work it out.

say: People were **frightened for nothing**, and I'd say so.
**Hard work** still counts, as I'd say at church.
think: AI already saves her about **five hours a week** on the cake stall.
With a **steady job**, four months saved and Ken's farm work, the household feels secure.
do: Keep **four days** at the supermarket, including the trainer role.
Add a **Sunday market** in the next town for the stall.
Save stall money in a **separate account** for a bakery.
S0.quote: Last year I did forty Christmas cakes and the AI kept track of who'd paid and who wanted marzipan.
fieldNote: Uses AI **daily**, but for her own business rather than the till.
Her worry is **butter prices**, a normal business pressure she shrugs off.
Traditional values sit easily with an **entrepreneurial** streak.

steps.text: Keep four days on the tills and training new starters
Add a Sunday cake stall at the next town's market
Use AI to track Christmas cake orders and payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn. At the supermarket I'd tell the new starters to get comfortable with the tools, not scared of them. Online I'd post about how I run the stall with AI, because some of the other stallholders keep asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the supermarket will want fewer people on the tills over time, and the head office will use AI for the rotas and the ordering. But my real future is the cakes, and AI makes a one-woman business much easier. So for me this is more good than bad, though I'd keep an eye on the till hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the extra time to grow the stall into online orders with delivery round the villages on Fridays. I'd buy a second-hand commercial oven, about eight hundred, so I can bake twice as much. And I'd talk to the store manager about whether my training role could grow into training staff on the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, a bit excited. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer people on the tills. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who's fifty-eight and does the mornings. He's a lovely man but he struggles with the self-checkout screens. I'd try to help him, but I can't stop head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the eight hundred come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the stall account, which has about eleven hundred in it. I wouldn't touch our household savings for it, Ken and I agreed that when we married. Business money stays business money.

say: It's a **chance** for people willing to work and learn.
I'd post how I run **the stall with AI**, because other stallholders ask.
think: The supermarket will want **fewer people** on the tills over time.
AI makes a **one-woman business** easier, so this is more good than bad for her.
do: Start **online orders** with Friday delivery round the villages.
Buy a second-hand **commercial oven** for about eight hundred.
Ask to grow her trainer role into **training on new systems**.
fieldNote: Sees her till job thinning but her **own business** growing.
Strict about **separating** business and household money, agreed with Ken.
Thinks of older colleague **Gary**, but accepts she can't stop head office.

steps.text: Launch online cake orders with Friday village deliveries
Buy a second-hand commercial oven for about eight hundred
Ask the store manager to train staff on new systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard and we should look after each other. At church we'd need to organise help for families, because some people in town will be hit badly. I'd also say anyone with a skill should be using it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the supermarket job goes around 2031 when robots can fill shelves and serve, and the AI side of my stall gets even better in 2028. The worry is everyone else having the same idea, every laid-off person in town making cakes. And Ken's farm job goes when robots can milk and muck out, so 2031 is a bad year for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard straight away, everything from the stall into the household pot, aiming for a year of bills by 2031. I'd look for a small shop unit to rent for the bakery, because a real shop is harder to copy than a stall. And I'd keep the supermarket job right up to the end, because a wage is a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the business, frightened about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone would make cakes. How would you stand out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being first and being known. I've been at that market three years, people know my lemon drizzle. If I have a shop with a name over the door before 2031, I'm the one people already trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ken that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we might be running a bakery together, and he'd laugh because he burns toast. But he could do the deliveries and the heavy lifting. We'd be a family business, which is what my grandparents had.

say: It'll be **hard**, and we should look after each other.
Anyone with **a skill** should be using it now.
think: Her till job goes around **2031**, while AI makes her stall even easier from 2028.
Husband Ken's **dairy job** also goes in 2031, a bad year for both of them.
do: Move all stall income into **household savings**, aiming for a year of bills.
Rent a **small shop unit** for the bakery before 2031.
Keep the **supermarket wage** right up to the end.
feel: **Anxious**: excited about the business, frightened about the town.
S2.quote: If I have a shop with a name over the door before 2031, I'm the one people already trust.
fieldNote: Uses the **three-year gap** to build a business before robots take both wages.
Fears **competition** from other laid-off people more than the machines.
Plans a **family business** with Ken, echoing her grandparents.

steps.text: Move all cake stall income into household savings
Rent a small shop unit for the bakery before 2031
Keep the supermarket job until robots replace the tills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something, so build it. At church I'd offer to help people write business plans with the AI, because I've done mine. At work I'd say it more gently, because not everyone wants to be their own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about right for me. I could have the bakery running properly by 2029 and leave the supermarket before the robots get there in 2034. Ken would have till about 2034 on the farm too, so there's time to bring him in slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd move to three days at the supermarket and open the bakery shop on Thursdays to Saturdays. I'd use the stall savings and a small bank loan, maybe five thousand, for the unit and the oven. By year three I'd hand in my notice at the supermarket and do the bakery full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It feels like the push I needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan is a risk. Are you comfortable with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as it's small and the shop pays it back. My dad borrowed for his van at my age and never regretted it. I'd rather owe the bank five thousand than wait for someone to decide my future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town could go quiet if lots of people lose work at once, and then nobody's buying lemon drizzle. That's the bit I can't control. I'd keep the shop small so it doesn't sink us.

say: **Five years** is time to build something, so build it.
I'd help people at church write **business plans** with AI.
think: She could have the **bakery running** by 2029, before robots reach the tills in 2034.
Ken has until **about 2034** on the farm, so he can join slowly.
do: Drop to **three days** at the supermarket and open the bakery Thursday to Saturday.
Take a **small bank loan**, about five thousand, for the unit and oven.
**Hand in notice** at the supermarket by year three.
feel: **Uneasy** but more excited than scared, like the push she needed.
S3.quote: I'd rather owe the bank five thousand than wait for someone to decide my future.
fieldNote: Comfortable with **measured risk**, citing her father's van loan.
Names the one risk she can't control: a **quiet town** if many lose work.
Plans to **leave the supermarket** on her own timing, not the robots'.

steps.text: Take a five-thousand bank loan for a bakery unit and oven
Hand in her supermarket notice by year three
Open the bakery shop Thursday to Saturday in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. At church and at work I'd say the same, plan now and you'll be fine. I'd probably say it more often than people want to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I'm happiest with. I can grow the stall into a shop at my own pace, and Ken and I can start a family without rushing. By 2039 the bakery should be well known in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supermarket job for a few more years and grow the stall with the second market. Around 2029 I'd open the shop, and Ken and I would try for our first baby around then. I'd keep using AI for the business side, and look at an AI-powered oven when they get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a family. Does the timing of the robots affect that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. With ten years, I'd want the children at school before the robots come, so that the shop and our income are steady by then. In the two-year picture I'd have waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside you see in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People in town getting comfortable and doing nothing. Then 2039 comes and they're all at my door asking for work. I'd help where I can, but I can't employ the whole town.

say: **Ten years** is plenty for anyone willing to work.
**Plan now** and you'll be fine, I'd tell people at church and at work.
think: This is her **happiest picture**: the stall can become a shop at her own pace.
She and Ken can **start a family** without rushing.
do: Keep the supermarket job a few more years and add **a second market**.
Try for a **first baby** around the same time.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd want the children at school before the robots come, so that the shop and our income are steady by then.
fieldNote: A long warning lets her match **family timing** to the business.
Worries about **complacency** in town, not about her own income.
Her calm comes from **owning the plan**, not from the job being safe.

steps.text: Keep supermarket shifts while adding a second weekend market
Open the bakery shop in town around 2029
Try for a first baby once the bakery opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ken and I would lose both wages around 2031 and I'd be building a shop in a town where half the people just lost their jobs. What would help is small business loans that are easy to get, and fewer forms for opening a food shop. And the church organising help for families, which I'd join.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd hire people. I would. If the bakery works, I'd hire the people from the tills first. Gary from the mornings would make a lovely counter man.

headlineQuote: If the bakery works, I'd hire the people from the tills first.
portrait: Wendy, 27, works the **tills** and trains new starters at the only big supermarket in her market town.
Married to Ken, a **dairy farm** hand, she runs a Saturday cake stall that she manages with AI every day.
She sees AI mostly as help for her **own business**, while expecting the till job to fade.
With less warning she fears **both wages** going around 2031; with more she opens a bakery on her own timing.
Her traditional faith and family values sit alongside a clear **appetite for risk**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both wages could go around 2031 in a town hit hard at once.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **small business loans** and fewer forms for food shops.
